title: Clinical Mastery: Evaluation of Painful Proptosis
summary: Painful proptosis is a clinical alarm bell requiring rapid differentiation between inflammatory, infectious, and neoplastic etiologies. This guide provides a systematic diagnostic and management framework for the ophthalmologist to avoid vision- and life-threatening outcomes.

sections.title: Definition & Clinical Significance
sections.content: Proptosis (exophthalmos) refers to the forward displacement of the globe. When accompanied by pain, it indicates active orbital disease, typically related to rapid volume expansion, inflammation, or infiltration of orbital tissues, necessitating urgent exclusion of orbital cellulitis, carotid-cavernous fistula, or malignancy.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Referral Criteria
content: RAPD (Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect) - signifies optic nerve compression.
Dyschromatopsia (Color vision loss on Ishihara plates).
Restrictive strabismus / Diplopia in primary gaze.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Protocol
content: Step 1: Complete ophthalmic exam (VAs, pupils, slit-lamp, fundus, motility).
Step 3: Imaging: Contrast-enhanced CT (for bones/sinuses) or MRI/MRA (for soft tissue/vascular).
Step 4: Labs: CBC, ESR, CRP, Thyroid panel (TSH, T3, T4, TRAb).
Step 5: Biopsy: If inflammatory/neoplastic process is suspected after imaging.

content.explanation: Mass: M-Moveability, R-Rate of growth, C-Consistency, A-Attachment/Adhesion, T-Tenderness.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: In Thyroid Eye Disease, the enlargement of EOMs classically SPARS the tendons, which helps differentiate it from myositis.
Always listen for a bruit in cases of proptosis; a subjective bruit is pathognomonic for CCF.
If an elderly patient presents with a painful orbital mass, assume lymphoma or metastatic disease until proven otherwise.
Management of orbital cellulitis requires aggressive IV antibiotic therapy (e.g., Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone) and surgical drainage if abscess is present.
Consider IgG4-related ophthalmic disease (IgG4-ROD) in patients with scleritis or dacryoadenitis.
